units.translation: οἱ κεκμηκότες [the wearied ones] or οἱ καμόντες [the toilers] the dead, as βροτῶν εἴδωλα καμόντων [the phantoms of toiling mortals] in Homer and οἱ κεκμηκότες [the wearied ones] in Plato and Aristotle and others indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 4 p. 923

The reading there is uncertain (τῶν πρὸ σὺ, μάρπτι [of those before you, Marptis] Hermann), where the scholiast says πρότερον θάνοις, ὦ μάρπτι, πρὶν ἡμᾶς συλλαβεῖν [may you die first, O Marptis, before seizing us].
the ship having toiled against the sea wave
to toil in exchange of speech
God loves to hasten with the one who toils
I will not weary of telling you the good things
the fruit of the earth and the flowing abundance of flocks, thriving for the citizens, not to weary in time
Zeus, most hospitable to the dead
may you die first, O Marptis, before seizing us
with which compare καμπὴ ὀξεῖα [sharp bend] the name of a place in Theophr. H. Pl. 4, 11, 8.
gladly would he bend his knee in his own home
for he must bend back the other leg of the double course toward home for safe return
I am bent by such misfortunes
by what misfortunes from him I am bent
bent by countless misfortunes and pains
bending the feet (in running), i.e. swift
bending the feet (in running), i.e. swift

on which see Ern. Curtius in the essay published at Berlin in 1869, "On the Kneeling Figures of Ancient Greek Art." The scholiast wrongly explains it as ή κάμπτουσα τῶν κολαζομένων τοὺς πόδας, οἱονεὶ ἡ συμποδίζουσα καὶ μὴ ἐῶσα φυγεῖν [she who bends the feet of those being punished, as it were she who shackles and does not allow to flee], just as Hesychius explains καμπεσίγουνος Ἑρινύς [knee-bending Erinys], a gloss taken from an unknown poet, as ἀπὸ τοῦ κάμπτειν τὰ γόνατα τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων [from bending the knees of sinners]. Schuetz rightly says: "It is one thing to bend the knee, which means to rest, another to bend the feet, which is to walk, to go, and therefore καμψίπους here means swift-footed." And so already Heath, who compares the epithet of the Erinyes δρομάδες [swift-running].
she who bends the feet of those being punished, as it were she who shackles and does not allow to flee
from bending the knees of sinners

which the scholiast explains as καναχηδόν δακρύετε [weep with resounding], and the gloss as ἠχητικόν [sounding]. The adjective is not read elsewhere: but related forms exist, καναχηδά καναχηδόν [with resounding], καναχή [clangor] and καναχίζω [to ring].
there is an Aetnaean beetle toiling with force
there is a city Canobus at the edge of the land
he came to Canobus and to Memphis
Capaneus, son of Hipponous, leader of the Argives
to trade, to act like a huckster
to trade, to act like a huckster
